claims.text: The initial rapidly processed alloy has a homogeneous, metastable solid-solution microstructure without significant intermetallic formation.
Thermal exposure transforms the metastable solid solution into a microstructure containing discrete Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
The transformation is driven by diffusion-controlled segregation of Mg.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitation proceeds through nucleation-and-growth behavior describable by Avrami-type kinetics.
Temperatures of 600–650 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere sufficiently activate Mg-associated diffusion to drive intermetallic nucleation and growth.
The size, distribution, volume fraction, and connectivity of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds mediate oxide-scale development.
Finely dispersed, isolated Mg-rich intermetallics promote a resilient, adherent, and more uniform oxide scale.
A fine, isolated intermetallic morphology retains or can improve high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the as-deposited state.
A fine, isolated intermetallic morphology retains or can improve corrosion resistance relative to the as-deposited state.
Coarse, interconnected Mg-rich intermetallic networks act as preferential oxidation sites or oxidation hot spots.
Intermetallics that coarsen and percolate along grain boundaries or interfaces disrupt protective oxide formation.
Intermetallic coarsening and interconnection beyond a critical threshold cause localized oxidation and accelerated corrosion.
The proposed behavior applies below temperatures that cause catastrophic phase instability or melting.
